issues.legal_issue: Trustees who obtained the benefit of a remand for adjudication on the merits cannot withdraw the proceedings so as to prevent that adjudication of a dispute concerning charitable trust property.
material_facts: Trustees sought court permission to sell property endowed for religious services, and the proceedings raised disputes about whether the property itself or only its income had been dedicated and which authority could permit a sale.
The Commissioner responsible for religious endowments asserted that the property was a specific endowment and that the required regulatory permission had not been obtained.

In an earlier appeal, the parties agreed to a fresh decision on the merits, and the Supreme Court ordered that decision; proceedings against the trustees were dropped in connection with that arrangement.
After the matter returned to the High Court, the trustees sought to withdraw both the permission application and the revision, which would have prevented the agreed merits adjudication.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have permitted withdrawal; the appeal was allowed and the matter remitted for decision on the merits and according to law.
issues.legal_principle: Order 23 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure ordinarily permits withdrawal where it does not nullify a finding on the merits in favour of the opposing party; the High Court correctly stated that general approach, reflected in Thakur Singh v. A. Achuta Rao, Kedar Nath v. Chandra Karan, V. Dube v. Harcharan, Charles Samuel v. Board of Trustees, Lala Chetram v. Krishnamoni, Jubedan Begum v. Sekhawat Ali Khan, Ram Dhan v. Jagat Prasad and related cases. But a party that has obtained a benefit on the basis of an agreed merits adjudication cannot then prevent that adjudication by withdrawing the proceedings. Courts also have parens patriae jurisdiction over charitable and religious trusts, and public interest may require adjudication of the dispute.

rule.if: trust_property_sale_permission_case and merits_remand_by_consent and trustees_received_benefit_from_remand and withdrawal_would_prevent_merits_adjudication

predicates.trust_property_sale_permission_case: Trustees brought a proceeding seeking permission to sell property held for charitable or religious purposes.
predicates.merits_remand_by_consent: The parties agreed that a dispute in the proceeding would be decided on its merits after remand.
predicates.trustees_received_benefit_from_remand: The trustees obtained a benefit after the matter was remanded on the basis of the agreed merits adjudication.
predicates.withdrawal_would_prevent_merits_adjudica: The trustees sought withdrawal that would prevent the agreed dispute from being decided on its merits.

issues.definition: When trustees seeking permission to sell charitable or religious property obtained a benefit through a consent-based remand for merits adjudication, they cannot withdraw the proceeding if withdrawal would prevent that adjudication.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may determine whether a subordinate court correctly decided the facts on which its jurisdiction depends and may obtain additional evidence needed to decide those facts.
material_facts: The District Court considered an application seeking permission to sell property held under a trust.
The parties disputed whether the trust deed dedicated the property itself or only charged its income, and whether the property was a specific endowment subject to a different permission process.
The trust deed was the central document bearing on the character of the property and the District Court had proceeded on the basis that it had jurisdiction.
The Commissioner had raised the jurisdictional objections in the record, and the parties might seek to adduce further evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could examine the jurisdictional facts in revision and, if necessary, receive further evidence itself or direct the District Court to record it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a High Court may examine whether a subordinate court correctly determined facts on which its jurisdiction depends. The Court relied on Chaube Jagdish Prasad v. Ganga Prasad, applying the principles stated in Queen v. Commissioner of Income Tax. The nature of the property determined whether the District Court could act under Section 34 of the Indian Trusts Act and whether permission under Section 34(1) of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act was implicated.

predicates.revision_proceeding: A party brought a revision challenging an order made by a subordinate court.
predicates.subordinate_court_jurisdiction_depends_o: Whether the subordinate court had authority to deal with the matter depends on disputed facts about the subject matter.
predicates.central_document_available: A document central to determining the subject matter's character is available for consideration.
predicates.additional_evidence_needed: The parties may need to provide further evidence to resolve the disputed jurisdictional facts.

issues.definition: In a revision, the High Court may decide disputed facts that determine the subordinate court's jurisdiction and may use a central document or obtain further evidence to do so.
